item.title: Ridding society of regressive norms
Nations commit to get nature goals back on track
item.description:
Nearly 200 nations struck hard-fought agreements Friday at a UN biodiversity summit, but the outcome was accompanied by disappointment over missed opportunities to address humanity’s destructive toll on nature.
Delegates cheered as crucial texts were approved in overtime but the celebrations were tempered by acrimonious debates and regret over limited progress on some of the most contentious issues.
The COP17 summit in Armenia sought to revive a landmark commitment to halt and reverse the destruction of nature by 2030 after global efforts to meet that goal fell short.
Over two bruising weeks in Yerevan, nations were urged to correct course to keep the pact alive and protect the plants, animals and ecosystems that sustain life on Earth.
The United Nations had warned that progress was insufficient to meet the goals of the 2030 target including protecting 30 percent of Earth’s land and oceans, tackling pollution and invasive species, and boosting money for conservation.
“And that’s it. Perfect,” said COP17 president Hambardzum Matevosyan in Armenia as he brought down the gavel on two major texts, the final versions of which were still not available early Saturday.
But the outcome was “not commensurate” with the crisis engulfing the natural world, said French Ecological Transition Minister Monique Barbut on Saturday.
“The progress we failed to achieve here is a series of missed opportunities to speed up our response to the loss of biodiversity,” Barbut said in a lengthy statement sent to AFP, stressing that “nature will not wait for the pace of our negotiations.”
The final plenary stretched through Friday night and well into the next morning, with negotiations turning sour as the hours dragged on.
Even as some delegates left to catch flights, others stayed behind to argue technical points.
Veteran COP observer Juliette Landry from the IDDRI think tank told AFP “there was a lot of push and pull in every direction” throughout the summit and “in that context, it’s hard to get things accepted.”
UN biodiversity chief Astrid Schomaker said the summit had achieved some “quite remarkable things at a moment when multilateralism is supposedly not functioning.”
“Some of these more difficult subjects, we could not expect to have strong negotiated commitments. That was never the plan,” she told reporters after the summit’s close.
In a draft agreement of one closely watched text, nations were urged to “accelerate” their efforts and warned that “increased action” was needed to tackle the forces driving biodiversity loss.
This “represents a positive outcome... and though there are weaknesses, particularly on harmful subsidies, it does represent a step forward,” Guido Broekhoven from WWF International told AFP.
Tackling subsidies and other incentives that encourage activities harmful to nature -- such as fossil fuels, intensive agriculture and overfishing -- was one of the most politically fraught agenda items at the summit.
“Even though the agreed decision text expresses it in weak terms, COP17 saw important political momentum to address harmful financial incentives, including subsidies,” An Lambrechts from Greenpeace International told AFP.
A rare fight over science cast a pall over the summit, with a number of countries accused of undermining efforts to approve key reports in scenes that shocked even seasoned negotiators.
“We regret the increasing instances in which scientific evidence and its uptake has been challenged or constrained” by politics, said Swiss negotiator Gabriela Blatter in a statement on behalf of dozens of countries.
“Our delegations fully respect every state’s right to safeguard national interest but science is not negotiable.”
A separate row revolved around finding new cash sources to fund conservation efforts -- another hot-button issue with public budgets under strain amid an energy crisis and conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East.
The European Union led a charge for wealthy emerging economies such as China to contribute to global conservation efforts, a contentious issue at COP17.
In a sign of possible compromise, another draft text that circulated Friday invited countries outside the developed-country donors to voluntarily join the group.
Outstanding questions over the design of the Cali Fund -- a UN mechanism that hoped to attract billions of dollars in corporate contributions but is close to empty -- were left unresolved.
“By punting essential decisions to two years from now, parties have all but ensured the fund remains empty until then,” said Pakhi Das from the nonprofit organization Plant-for-the-Planet.
The COP17 summit decided early Saturday that Ecuador would host the next biodiversity talks in 2028 after the South American nation defeated rival candidate Panama in a secret vote.

item.title: Bollywood and the underworld — together in the spotlight?
item.description:
“In the entire film industry, whoever works without aligning with us, or works with Salman Khan, will be killed.”
This warning was delivered in an audio message by presumed attackers on Indian actor Tiger Shroff in Mumbai earlier this month, as they claimed responsibility for the shooting.
The apparent perpetrators said they were connected to Lawrence Bishnoi, a student-politician-turned-gangster who has been in prison since 2014. Notably, police have not confirmed the gang’s involvement.
The shots fired at Shroff, which injured his driver, were only the latest in a string of attacks targeting prominent figures from the Mumbai-based film industry, popularly known as “Bollywood.”
Since 2022, gunmen fired shots at actor Salman Khan’s apartment and at the home of filmmaker Rohit Shetty in Mumbai, as well as actor Disha Patani’s family home in northern India. Actor Ranveer Singh also reportedly received an extortion demand of nearly $1.1 million.
The attacks have spread to the other side of the globe, with a cafe owned by comedian Kapil Sharma in Surrey, Canada, also hit three times.
For an industry that once lived in the shadow of organized crime, the attacks have revived old fears, harking back to the crime bosses of the 1990s. But experts say the threat facing Bollywood today looks very different from the one it faced three decades ago.
In the 1990s, Mumbai’s underworld was deeply entangled with the Hindi film industry.
“The mafia was always fascinated with the movie industry,” said S Hussain Zaidi, crime journalist and author of “Dongri to Dubai: Six Decades of the Mumbai Mafia,” who has covered organized crime in the city for over three decades.
Gangsters like Dawood Ibrahim, Abu Salem and Chhota Shakeel “were totally obsessed” with Bollywood, he told DW, much like mafiosi who sought a foothold in Hollywood.
To the gangsters, films offered glitz and glamor, but also a way to launder their profits. They invested in films “so that they could control the industry and have a legitimate way of making money,” Zaidi added.
When producers didn’t cooperate, the consequences could be fatal. In 1997, music mogul Gulshan Kumar, founder of the label T-Series, was shot dead. In 2000, filmmaker Rakesh Roshan, father of Bollywood star Hrithik Roshan, was shot and wounded.
Mumbai’s streets were “made red with blood” in 1998, Zaidi said, describing the year as the pinnacle of gang killings.
D Sivanandhan, the former Police Commissioner of Mumbai, who led the crackdown, says 101 businessmen were shot dead in 1998 alone, or one “every third day,” mostly over unpaid extortion demands.
Police efforts were reinforced by a tough new organized crime law passed in 1999, which Sivanandhan calls the “ultimate weapon.” Security forces used electronic surveillance and preventive detention, and seized some 2,500 illegal weapons.
“A few encounters also happened, but that is not a policy nor a strategy,” he told DW, referring to police shootouts.
By the early 2000s, the gangs’ hold had been broken, and a new Mumbai seemed to be emerging.
The man believed to be behind the latest wave of attacks is not from Mumbai.
Bishnoi, 33, comes from a landowning family in the northern state of Punjab and was studying in Chandigarh when he was drawn into violent student politics. Then, he was arrested, incarcerated and eventually turned to crime, says journalist Jupinderjit Singh, author of “Gangs of Punjab.”
“He was introduced to the University of Crime through the jail,” Singh told DW.
Bishnoi went on to build what Singh describes as one of the first criminal syndicates spanning several northern Indian states. Investigators say he still directs operations from prison using concealed phones and messaging apps.
Currently, Bishnoi is held in a jail in Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s home state of Gujarat.
His network stretches beyond India’s borders. In September 2025, Canada designated the Bishnoi gang a terrorist entity. Last month, the FBI added Satinderjeet Singh, popularly known as Goldy Brar, to its Ten Most Wanted list, offering up to $1 million for information leading to his arrest. US prosecutors described him as the alleged leader of Bishnoi’s group in North America.
While Bishnoi comes from an affluent landowning family, his shooters are mostly poor. The gang usually recruits them online.
“There are so many youngsters who want to do something… they are just pulled by the lore attached to Lawrence Bishnoi,” Singh explained. “Recruiting is no big issue… They offer money, protection, weapons.”
For Bishnoi, it seems personal.
In 1998, Salman Khan was accused of killing a blackbuck, an antelope revered by Bishnoi’s community. Bishnoi vowed revenge, and many of the attacks targeted people close to the actor, including the 2024 killing of politician Baba Siddique, which police have linked to the gang.
Singh sees the feud as a bid for respectability. Criminals “always try to find something that makes them a moral guardian,” he says, and this case was Bishnoi’s “chance to redeem himself.”
But money and intimidation matter too.
“Bollywood has a lot of money,” Singh added, pointing that the previous generation of gangsters was no longer in position to take advantage.
“With Dawood Ibrahim and his counterparts away, there was a vacuum, and Lawrence Bishnoi is trying to exploit that.”
Sivanandhan explained the old Mumbai gangs ran a whole “basket” of illegal businesses, from smuggling to protection rackets and cricket match-fixing. Their members were “local boys,” while the Bishnoi gang has “nothing to do with Mumbai,” he added. It targets Bollywood because the industry is “loaded with money” and a “soft underbelly.”
“They are using Bollywood as an ATM,” he told DW. “Insert a card and collect your money.”
Meanwhile, Zaidi sees the attacks mainly as publicity. “It’s a way to grab headlines,” he told DW. Within hours of the recent attack on Shroff, someone claimed on social media that he was targeted for being close to Khan, a logic Zaidi called “absolutely illogical and absurd.”
But publicity is useful to gangs that live off extortion. “The base material of extortion is: create fear,” a security professional responsible for the protection of several Bollywood stars, who asked not to be named because of the sensitivity of the issue, told DW.
Still, experts say its hard to argue that the ongoing violence is comparable to the 1990s crime wave.
“I won’t say resurgence, because that would be a bit of an exaggeration,” Zaidi said. In the 1990s, several rival gangs fought for control of Mumbai. Today, other than Bishnoi’s faction, other gangs are not considered active in Mumbai.
The film industry is also not paying up the way it once did, because the shift to digital payments has made large cash transactions hard to hide, he added.
Sivanandhan disagrees. The shootings at walls and gates, followed by quick claims on social media, are “all aimed at collecting… extortion money,” he said. In his view, “cash-rich Bollywood would be coughing up so much, which is enough to run an army of people.”
At any case, the fear remains real.
And even if violence is not as prevalent, hundreds of thousands of people rely on the Mumbai film industry for their livelihoods.
“If the fear of the underworld continues, leading names may be forced to leave Mumbai,” the All Indian Cine Workers Association (AICWA) President Suresh Shyamlal Gupta wrote to Home Minister Amit Shah.
“Mumbai will not be allowed to go back to the underworld days of the 1990s, and Bollywood will not be allowed to work in the shadow of fear,” Gupta wrote.
With security forces seemingly on the back foot, gangsters are likely to continue their campaign.
Several Bollywood stars have already stepped up their security.

item.title: Rajshahi district leads board in pass rate, GPA-5
item.description:
Rajshahi district has topped the eight districts under the Rajshahi Education Board in both pass rate and the number of students securing GPA-5 in this year’s Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) examinations.
Despite Rajshahi’s strong performance, the overall results of the board were disappointing, with the pass rate falling to 45.06% this year. More than half of the students who appeared for the examinations failed.
Girls, however, outperformed boys in both pass rate and GPA-5 achievements.
Only nine colleges across the eight districts recorded a 100% pass rate, while no student from 39 colleges passed.
Rajshahi Education Board Controller of Examinations Professor Iffat Zerin announced the results at 11:00am on Saturday.
According to the board, 4,520 students secured GPA-5 this year. Of them, 1,785 were from Rajshahi district, accounting for nearly 39.5% of all GPA-5 achievers under the board.
Bogra ranked second with 1,309 GPA-5 achievers, followed by Pabna with 550.
Rajshahi also recorded the highest pass rate at 55.33%. Bogra ranked second at 53.64%, while Joypurhat stood third at 41.67%.
A total of 141,936 students registered for this year’s HSC examinations under the Rajshahi Education Board. Of them, 137,356 appeared, with 61,894 passing and 75,462 failing.
In Rajshahi district, 28,086 students appeared for the examinations, of whom 15,540 passed.
Students from 743 colleges across the board’s eight districts took the examinations at 208 centres.
Girls recorded a pass rate of 53.03%, compared with 37.71% for boys. Of the 4,520 GPA-5 achievers, 2,555 were girls and 1,965 were boys.
Professor Iffat Zerin said 31 examinees were expelled for adopting unfair means during the examinations.
She said only nine colleges recorded a 100% pass rate, while 39 colleges had no students passing.

item.title: Heading to Saint Martin’s this week? Here’s how to reach the island
item.description:
Tourists flock to Saint Martin’s Island every year, drawn by its natural beauty. After a long wait, the country’s only coral island is set to reopen to tourists on November 1.
Although tourism activities will resume on the island, ships will not operate during the first five days. Ship services are scheduled to begin on November 6.
This naturally raises a question: how will tourists reach Saint Martin’s Island during these five days?
According to available information, tourists will have to rely on trawlers or speedboats to travel to the island during this period. This means that those planning to visit Saint Martin’s Island between November 1 and 5 will have to use these alternative watercraft.
However, travel by trawler or speedboat will depend heavily on weather conditions, the state of the sea, and permission from the relevant authorities.
This raises several questions. If tourists can travel to the island by trawlers or speedboats, then what is the need for regular ship services?
Travelling by ship may take comparatively longer and cost more. Yet ships hold a different kind of importance for tourists: safety and a relatively stable journey.
For sea travel, larger vessels are generally considered safer and more comfortable than trawlers or smaller speedboats. This is particularly important when the sea is rough, as travelling in smaller vessels can become risky.
So, why will ship services begin five days later?
One of the main reasons is that the vessels concerned have not yet received the necessary clearance from the Department of Environment.
Ship operations are expected to begin on November 6, once the required clearance and other formalities have been completed.
In other words, although the island will reopen to tourists, ship services cannot begin immediately because the approval process is still underway.
Regulating tourism has always been important for protecting the environment and biodiversity of Saint Martin’s Island.
Therefore, before planning a trip, tourists should check the approved modes of transportation, ship schedules, and the latest instructions from the relevant authorities.
Those planning to visit during the first five days should be particularly careful and confirm the safety of travelling by trawler or speedboat, check the weather forecast, and ensure that all necessary permissions are in place before setting out.
The doors to Saint Martin’s Island will reopen on November 1, but tourists will have to wait another five days for regular ship services.
So, before heading to the island, keep in mind not only the travel date but also the mode of transportation and safety arrangements.

item.title: Does charging your phone overnight damage the battery?
item.description:
For many people, putting the phone on charge before bed and unplugging it in the morning is a regular habit. But once the battery hits 100%, many wonder whether keeping it connected to power for hours on end causes damage. With modern smartphones, though, the matter is a little different.
Today’s smartphones usually use lithium-ion or lithium-polymer batteries. Once the phone is fully charged, its charging system reduces the current supplied as needed or shuts off the main charging process. So even after reaching 100%, power does not keep flowing into the battery in the same way. The idea that leaving a phone on charge overnight will “overcharge” and ruin it is therefore not correct.
Even without overcharging, keeping a battery at full charge for a long time is not ideal. In lithium-based batteries, holding a full charge for long periods can gradually speed up chemical degradation. Over time, this affects the battery’s maximum capacity.
As a result, after months or years of use, you may notice the phone’s charge running out faster than before. In other words, the biggest concern with charging overnight is not instant “overcharging,” but a somewhat faster decline in the battery’s health over the long term.
Temperature matters a great deal for batteries. While it is normal for a phone to get a little warm while charging, excessive heat can put extra stress on the battery.
In particular, you should not charge the phone under a pillow, blanket, or bedding. In such places, there is little airflow around the phone, so heat cannot escape easily. It is a safer habit to charge the phone on a hard, flat, open surface.
To help preserve battery life, many smartphones now come with special charging features. Depending on the phone, these may be called Optimized Charging, Adaptive Charging, or Battery Protection.
These features analyze the user’s charging habits and often avoid holding the phone at 100% for long, instead completing the full charge closer to a set time. This reduces the amount of time the battery spends fully charged.
So, is it fine to sleep with the phone on charge?
Because modern smartphones have multiple safeguards that control charging, leaving the phone plugged in overnight generally won’t cause immediate damage. However, to keep the battery healthy in the long run, it is best to avoid overheating and keep features such as Optimized Charging or Battery Protection enabled.
Remember, a smartphone battery is a consumable component. Even with good care, its capacity will decline over time. The idea that a battery is ruined only because of overnight charging is not correct. Rather, temperature, usage patterns, and the age of the battery all combine to determine how long it lasts.

item.title: Try these five tricks to stop overpaying for your AC
item.description:
As temperatures continue to rise, staying comfortable indoors has become increasingly difficult. From ceiling fans and air coolers to air conditioners, people are relying on different cooling solutions to cope with the heat. However, running an air conditioner for extended periods can raise concerns about electricity costs, particularly among middle-income households.
Many people limit their use of air conditioners at night to avoid high electricity bills, often compromising their comfort in the process. However, with a few adjustments to everyday habits, it is possible to maintain a comfortable indoor temperature while managing energy consumption.
Here are some practical ways to make your air conditioner more energy-efficient.
The temperature setting plays an important role in determining how much electricity an air conditioner consumes. Lower settings require the compressor to work harder and for longer periods, increasing energy use.
According to a recent study cited in the original report, each degree of reduction in the temperature setting can increase electricity consumption by around 6%. Keeping the thermostat at a moderate temperature, therefore, can help reduce unnecessary energy use.
Setting the air conditioner to 18°C may seem like an effective way to cool a room quickly, but it can significantly increase energy consumption. A setting of 24°C is generally sufficient to maintain a comfortable indoor environment during hot weather.
Instead of lowering the temperature excessively, gradually adjust your nighttime settings to 24°C. This can help maintain comfort while reducing the strain on the air conditioner's cooling system.
An air conditioner works more efficiently when cool air remains inside the room. Open doors, poorly sealed windows, and gaps around frames allow cool air to escape while letting warm air enter.
Make sure all doors and windows are properly closed before switching on the AC. Check for gaps that may need sealing and use curtains to reduce heat entering through windows.
Electronic appliances generate heat while operating, which can increase the cooling load on an air conditioner. Televisions, computers, and other devices can contribute to indoor heat, making the AC work harder to maintain the desired temperature.
Switch off appliances that are not in use before going to bed. This can help reduce unnecessary heat generation and improve cooling efficiency.
Running an air conditioner throughout the night may not always be necessary. As the room cools down, maintaining the same level of cooling until morning can lead to unnecessary electricity consumption.
Use the timer function to schedule the AC to switch off one or two hours before your usual wake-up time, if the room remains comfortable. This can help avoid excessive cooling and reduce operating time.
With the right temperature settings, proper room insulation, and mindful use of household appliances, you can enjoy a cooler night's sleep without putting unnecessary pressure on your electricity bill.

item.title: Hakimi bags hat-trick as PSG rip Le Havre to pieces
item.description:
Achraf Hakimi rose to the occasion scoring a glorious hat-trick on Friday as a heavily rotated Paris Saint-Germain thumped rock-bottom Le Havre 5-1 in Ligue 1.
PSG's nearest Ligue 1 rivals Rennes lost 5-2 at Nice dropping four points adrift while Olivier Giroud's late goal lifted Lille second after their 1-0 home win over Lens.
The former World Cup and Champions League winner Giroud is now 40 and the giant striker was flushed red with pleasure after his 86th minute shot settled a tense, tight struggle.
PSG top the table with 20 points after nine games, Lille are second on 18, Monaco can join them should they beat Paris FC on Sunday, while Rennes have 16.
On just two points so far Le Havre gave PSG a game early on as they suddenly surged forward in numbers with the PSG backline scampering in retreat before striker Josh Maja hammered in the opener against the run of play on 18 minutes.
Pushing for a second, Le Havre were carved open in a quick-fire move with Belgian winger Mika Godts racing onto a Hakimi through-ball to level on 26 minutes.
Two minutes later Hakimi left the defence trailing and his blistering low drive just inside the near post made it 2-1.
The European champions were running the Normandy side ragged before Hakimi scored his second with a fierce free-kick that curled low past the 'keeper Arnaud Bodard to put PSG 3-1 up.
On a lightning break the hosts poured everyone forward in a brave but naive effort to get back into the game, only for PSG to burst back, catching the home goalkeeper way off his line with not a single defender in his half.
Senny Mayulu ran around the horrified stopper, and his cool long-range finish hit the back of the net with nobody in the box effectively ending the contest, just after the hour.
Hakimi's hat-trick arrived when he threaded a shot through a forest of players on 69 minutes and had hardly finished a triumphant celebration when coach Luis Enrique subbed him off.
"He's a striker when we have the ball. He's free to do that when we are in possession, but obliged to defend when we aren't," said Luis Enrique.
The Spanish coach left stars Desire Doue, Vitinha and Joao Neves on the bench while Ousmane Dembele and Georgian attacker Khvicha Kvaratskhelia were missing through injury.

item.title: India opposition parties hold mock impeachment of poll chief
item.description:
India's political opposition staged a symbolic impeachment of the election commissioner on Saturday to protest against a revision of voter lists that they say could unfairly benefit the ruling party.

The nationwide revision of electoral rolls has sparked political disputes and street protests in the world's largest democracy over the last month.

The Election Commission says the initiative is necessary to ensure accurate voter lists, but the opposition claims it is being manipulated to favour Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

“We will ensure Gyanesh Kumar resigns”: Abhijeet Dipke says "ready to go to jail" ahead of march

Both the Election Commission and the BJP deny the allegations.

On Saturday, opposition parties gathered at the residence of Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge in the capital New Delhi, re-enacting a parliamentary session.

They held mock impeachment proceedings, which have no constitutional or legal force, against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

"The motion we have brought forward today is aimed at safeguarding the dignity of a constitutional institution," Kharge said.

"Our intention is for the Election Commission to function impartially, in line with the spirit of the constitution."

Under the constitution, the chief election commissioner can only be removed through a parliamentary process requiring a special majority.

Senior Congress leader Rahul Gandhi said the opposition had resorted to the symbolic exercise as they "have nowhere else to go".

"We have no other option. Every single institution... is closed for us," Gandhi said.

In pictures: Indian protesters call for election chief to resign

The event came a day before a major opposition rally in Delhi backed by the Cockroach Janta Party, an online youth-led movement that also supports the campaign against the voter-roll revision.

Home Minister Amit Shah said the BJP was ready to hold a special session of parliament to discuss the revision.

"But they (the opposition) have no intention of speaking there. They refuse to let the parliament function. Instead, they just create a ruckus," he said.

item.title: Workers clash with police repeatedly in Gazipur, 30 injured 15 vehicles vandalised
item.description:
Readymade Garment workers demonstrating on the roads in Gazipur, demanding a minimum monthly wage of Tk 30,000, clashed repeatedly with law enforcement agencies. At least 30 people were injured in the clashes. At least 15 vehicles, including a police vehicle, were vandalised. In response to the situation, 20 factories declared a holiday.

At around 2:30 pm today, Saturday, workers from the Interstoff factory began protesting after taking to the road in the Chandra Palli Bidyut area of Kaliakair upazila in Gazipur. Workers from several other nearby factories also joined the demonstration later. This caused severe traffic congestion on the Dhaka–Tangail highway.

The protesting workers said it had become difficult to run their households on their current wages. Opportunities for overtime work have also declined. Meanwhile, the prices of all essential commodities have increased, but their wages have remained unchanged. They said they had been demanding a minimum wage of Tk 30,000 for a long time.

Garment workers block Mirpur-10 demanding Tk 30,000 as wage

Aminul Islam, a lineman at Interstoff Apparel Limited, said, “The wages we earn after working hard all day are no longer enough to run our households. The prices of everything, including rice, lentils and oil, have gone up. Yet our wages remain where they were. We have been forced to take to the streets. We want to work, but we also need wages that allow us to support our families.”

Parveen Akter, a sewing operator at the same factory, said, “We are struggling to manage house rent, grocery bills and our children’s education. We used to earn some extra money through overtime, but those opportunities have also become limited. A monthly wage of Tk 30,000 has been our demand for a long time. If our demand is not met we will continue our movement.”

Industrial police, factory workers and local residents said workers had been protesting for higher wages in various areas of Gazipur, including Konabari and Mouchak, for the past two weeks. Meanwhile, the government has decided to form a new wage board to increase workers’ wages. Despite this, labour unrest has continued at various factories.

Md Ashrafuzzaman, organising secretary, Jatiya Garments Sramik Jote BangladeshA demand had been made for the immediate formation of a new wage board for garment workers. Workers are demanding a minimum wage of Tk 30,000. However they must carry out their programmes peacefully.

At noon on Saturday, after the lunch break, workers at the Interstoff factory did not return to work and instead took up positions on the Dhaka–Tangail highway. They then blocked the road by dumping sacks of rubbish from the surrounding area onto it. At one point, workers from the nearby Divine Textile factory also joined them.

Labour unrest subsequently spread to various factories between Chandra and Konabari. In response to the situation, factory authorities declared holidays at 20 factories. Some of the workers sent home also joined the protests.

After receiving the news, local police and industrial police went to the scene and tried to bring the situation under control by reasoning with the workers. The blockade began at 2:30 pm, causing severe inconvenience to passengers and transport workers.

At around 5:30 pm, police began using batons to clear the workers from the highway. At the time there were chases and counter chases that eventually escalated into clashes between the police and the workers. During the clashes, 15 vehicles were vandalised, including a police vehicle whose front windscreen was smashed.

Police began firing tear gas shells at around 7:00 pm. After the workers eventually moved away from the highway, traffic resumed on the Dhaka–Tangail highway at around 7:30 pm. Kaliakair Police Station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Shahidul Islam said 30 people including workers and police personnel had been injured in the clashes and counter-chases.

The injured workers received treatment at various local clinics. Kabir Hossain, a worker at Divine Textile, said, “Twenty to 25 of our workers were injured by police baton charges. Many others were injured by tear gas shells. Even if we leave today, our movement will resume tomorrow (Sunday) morning.”

Traffic disruption caused by blockade

Earlier in the afternoon, Harun Mia, a bus driver, spoke to Prothom Alo at the Chandra intersection. He said, “I have been stuck in the Chandra area for more than an hour. The same thing happened last Thursday. What are we supposed to do if garment workers keep blocking the roads like this?”

Passenger Md Kader Mia said, “I need to go to Dhaka for urgent work. After reaching Chandra, I was forced to get off the bus and continue on foot.”

Police disperse garment workers after nearly 4-hour road blockade in Uttara

Mohammad Ashrafuzzaman, organising secretary of the central committee of the Jatiya Garments Sramik Jote Bangladesh, said a demand had been made for the immediate formation of a new wage board for garment workers. Workers are demanding a minimum wage of Tk 30,000.

However, he said, they must carry out their programmes peacefully. He urged workers to refrain from programmes that could damage lives and property or cause public suffering.

Gazipur Industrial Police Superintendent Md Amzad Hossain said factory authorities had declared holidays at least at 20 factories between Chandra and Konabari because of the workers’ protests. Additional police personnel had been deployed at various locations to ensure security.

item.title: 28 prominent citizens: Jamaat, which opposed independence, cannot decide who is a freedom fighter
item.description:
Twenty-eight prominent citizens have expressed condemnation, concern and anger over the recent incident in Pirojpur in which Jamaat-e-Islami obstructed the burial of freedom fighter Manik Pashari and the provision of a state guard of honour. They said the incident has caused deep concern and anger among the public.

His burial was delayed for nearly 15 hours amid obstruction by local Jamaat-e-Islami leaders and activists. Only the state has the authority to determine whether someone officially recognised as a freedom fighter is indeed one. A party that opposed the country’s independence cannot decide, at any level, who is a freedom fighter and who is not, they said.

Freedom fighter Manik Pashari’s burial in Pirojpur: Relatives and locals recount events

The statement said the situation that arose in Pirojpur following the death of freedom fighter Manik Pashari on 24 October, and the arrangements for his guard of honour and burial, was deeply regrettable, undesirable and reprehensible. According to information from various sources, after the grave was dug for the first time, local Jamaat-e-Islami leaders and activists had it filled in.

Later, at around 2:00 am, Manik Pashari’s daughter and two sisters dug the grave again with the help of village police, using the light from mobile phones. His burial was completed under police protection, nearly 15 hours after his death. Fifty-five years after independence, such circumstances surrounding the final farewell to a freedom fighter raise profound questions and concerns about our state, society and political culture, said the statement.

Ministry forms committee to investigate incident involving Manik Pashari in Pirojpur

The signatories said freedom fighter Manik Pashari, a resident of Chitalia village in Shankarpasha Union of Pirojpur Sadar Upazila, had been staying at his daughter’s home in Gopalganj since the mass uprising of 5 August 2024. He died there on 24 October. In accordance with state rules, arrangements were made for his burial with a guard of honour as a freedom fighter.

However, Jamaat-e-Islami, the party that opposed the Liberation War during the country’s great struggle for independence, obstructed his burial by questioning whether he was a freedom fighter, they added.

The statement said, “Burial after a person’s death is a fundamental human right. No individual or group, not even the state, can violate this right. His body was subsequently taken to the Pirojpur Police Lines, where he was given a guard of honour. According to information available, his burial was delayed for nearly 15 hours amid obstruction by local Jamaat-e-Islami leaders and activists.”

Blocking burial while in opposition, what will they do if in power, asks Tasnim Jara

“Naturally, the question arises: only the state has the authority to determine whether someone officially recognised as a freedom fighter is indeed one. The state may verify this if it ever considers such a step necessary. A party that opposed independence cannot decide, at any level, who is a freedom fighter and who is not,” added the statement.

The statement said that the party had not only opposed independence and the Liberation War in 1971, but that documentary evidence had established allegations of war crimes, including the killing of intellectuals, against many of its leaders. To this day, they have neither acknowledged responsibility for those crimes nor offered even a minimal public apology for opposing the Liberation War.

The signatories believe that what was done to Manik Pashari amounted to a criminal offence. They said, “Obstructing a person’s funeral prayers and burial because of their political views or past role is in no way acceptable. Giving the dead a proper and dignified burial is a religious obligation and a fundamental teaching of Islam and all other religions.”

If they do this in opposition, what will they do in power: Tasnim Jara

“We have no words to express our condemnation of the disrespect shown to Manik Pashari in disregard of these teachings. We strongly demand that those involved in such criminal offences be brought to justice through a proper investigation and that appropriate and stringent legal action be taken against them,” they said.

The statement was signed by Sultana Kamal, Rasheda K Choudhury, Khushi Kabir, ZI Khan Panna, Iftekharuzzaman, Shaheen Anam, Rehnuma Ahmed, Shahidul Alam, Swapan Adnan, Shamsul Huda, Tabarak Hossain, Samina Luthfa, Sumaiya Khair, Tanzimuddin Khan, Robaet Ferdous, Zobaida Nasreen, Nova Ahmed, Zakir Hossain, Subrata Chowdhury, Salma Ali, Md Nur Khan, Pavel Partha, Rozina Begum, Saidur Rahman, Saeed Ahmed, Dipayan Khisa, Hana Shams Ahmed and Muktasree Chakma.

item.title: HSC: Exam dates for students who failed 1 or 2 subjects to be announced by 3 November
item.description:
Students who failed one or two subjects in this year's Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) and equivalent examinations will have an opportunity to retake only the subjects they failed within the next month.

Professor Syed Akhtaruzzaman, president of the Inter-Education Board Coordination Committee and chairman of the Dhaka Education Board, told Prothom Alo on Saturday that details regarding the examination dates, form-fill-up schedule and fees for these students would be announced by 3 November.

However, a source at the Dhaka Education Board said preliminary discussions were underway on whether the examinations could be held on 2 December. Authorities are also considering publishing the results within December so that successful candidates can have the opportunity to seek admission to higher education.

HSC results 2026 re-scrutiny applications open from Sunday

Under the existing system, students who fail one or more subjects in public examinations such as the SSC and HSC must wait a year to retake the examinations. They can sit for only the subjects they failed or choose to retake all subjects. As a result, students who fail just one or two subjects have to wait an entire year for another opportunity.

This year, a total of 422,905 candidates failed in one or two subjects. Of them, 298,040 failed in one subject, while 124,865 failed in two subjects.

At an event organised on Saturday to announce the results, Education Minister ANM Ehsanul Hoque Milon and Prime Minister's Adviser Mahdi Amin said students who failed one or two subjects in this year's HSC and equivalent examinations would be given an opportunity to retake the examinations within the next month.

item.title: Our education must move beyond grades
item.description:
We understand the immediate concern that comes from the drastic decline in this year’s Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) and equivalent examination pass rate.
Dropping by 6.71% down to 52.12%, alongside hundreds of thousands of failures, and institutions recording zero pass rates will inevitably trigger panicked headlines across the country. This newspaper has been no different.
On the surface, such a significant drop cannot simply be brushed aside as an administrative quirk. It is only natural to wonder what has happened for the number of students securing a GPA-5 to fall from 145,911 in 2024 to 40,084 in 2026 -- a drop of more than 72%.
Yet, reacting with reflexive hand-wringing or frantic attempts to massage the numbers misses the deeper, more vital reality.
For decades, our education system has prioritized pass rates and inflated GPA-5 tallies, fostering a culture of rote memorization, coaching-centre dependency, and superficial evaluation that has left our students fundamentally unequipped for the real world.
When students emerge from 12 years of schooling unable to analyze, adapt, or compete in a modernizing global economy, chasing a GPA-5 becomes a hollow and deceptive pursuit.
The state, educators, and parents must stop treating board exams as a bureaucratic obstacle course and start interrogating the structural "whys" behind our chronic learning deficits -- including acute teacher shortages, outdated curricula, and an assessment system that penalizes analytical thought.
Tackling our education crisis requires the government to look beyond annual statistical fluctuations. We need an overhaul of our education culture, one that pivots away from rote memorization toward competency-based education.
A 52% pass rate is a harsh wake-up call, but it should not be treated as a disaster to be masked by artificial grading leniency. Instead, it must serve as the catalyst to dismantle prioritizing grades over all.
It is time to stop chasing cosmetic metrics and finally invest in our youth's future by having an education system that builds capable, well-rounded citizens equipped to excel in life.

item.title: Restoring peace to the hills
item.description:
The recurring clashes and exchanges of gunfire between rival armed groups in Sajek potentially signal a resurgence of instability in the Chittagong Hill Tracts (CHT) that must not be taken lightly.
We should not be tolerating territorial rivalries erupting into open gunbattles as innocent local residents are forced to live in constant terror. This is equally true for tourism, local economies, and public safety which are repeatedly held hostage.
Such lawlessness cannot be treated as an inevitable feature of the region; bringing lasting peace, security, and the rule of law to the hills must become an immediate, non-negotiable priority.
For far too long, armed factions in the CHT have continued to operate, waging turf wars for political dominance. All the while, it has been civilian populations that have been affected.
Recent blockades, attacks on tourist convoys, and armed standoffs not only imperil local livelihoods but also directly challenge state authority. Law enforcement and security personnel stating that they struggle to access remote clash sites while communities are caught in the crossfire is simply not enough of a reason.
Peace in the CHT cannot be sustained through temporary ceasefires or passive monitoring from a distance. While political dialogue, genuine socio-economic development, and the full implementation of structural commitments remain vital for long-term reconciliation, the immediate priority must also be to ensure the safety and security of those who call the region home.
The people of the Chittagong Hill Tracts deserve safety, dignity, and economic progress, not perpetual warfare. It is time for the government to commit to the region, first by restoring peace.

item.title: Lack of ICU at National Eye Hospital delays surgery for heart patients
item.description:
Mustafa Kamal, a man in his 60s from Shikarpur village in Uzirpur upazila of Barisal, travelled to the National Institute of Ophthalmology and Hospital in Dhaka for treatment of an eye condition. Following a series of tests, doctors diagnosed a tumour in his eye socket (orbit) and recommended surgery.
However, his history of heart disease complicated the procedure. Doctors said he might require intensive monitoring after surgery. But the hospital, one of the country's leading specialised public eye care facilities, does not have an intensive care unit (ICU). As a result, he was advised to undergo the operation at another hospital.
Kamal said his surgery was initially scheduled at the National Institute of Ophthalmology and Hospital. However, the absence of ICU facilities meant the procedure could not be performed there.
He was advised to seek treatment at another medical college hospital. He subsequently contacted Dhaka Medical College Hospital, Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College Hospital and Mugda Medical College Hospital but failed to secure an operation date.
After visiting several hospitals over a number of days, he was told by Dhaka Medical College Hospital that he would have to wait nearly two months for surgery.
Kamal said he had met another heart patient while seeking treatment at the eye hospital. Unable to undergo surgery there, the patient eventually had the procedure at a private hospital.
Kamal said he had met another heart patient while seeking treatment at the eye hospital. Unable to undergo surgery there, the patient eventually had the procedure at a private hospital.
"I do not have the financial means to undergo surgery at a private hospital," he said.
Like Kamal, other patients with heart conditions are struggling to access complex eye surgery because of the absence of ICU facilities at the specialised hospital.
Although the hospital offers a wide range of surgical services, it lacks an ICU. Doctors said some patients require general anaesthesia and close monitoring after surgery, making intensive care support necessary in certain cases. Without such facilities, they have to be referred to other hospitals.
Patients said transferring to another hospital means going through fresh registration, securing a new appointment and undergoing additional tests. This delays treatment and increases the financial and emotional burden on patients and their families.
Doctors, however, said not all eye surgeries require ICU support. Routine cataract operations can generally be performed without intensive care facilities. However, depending on a patient's physical condition, the type of surgery and the anaesthesia required, some complex procedures may necessitate close monitoring.
Patients with heart conditions, in particular, require additional precautions before and after surgery, they said.
Dr Sayeed Mehboob Ul Qadir, director of the National Institute of Ophthalmology and Hospital, told Dhaka Tribune that the hospital had never had an ICU since its establishment. He recently assumed office and is working to address patients' basic healthcare needs.
"I cannot comment on matters that predate my joining. The hospital provides necessary surgical procedures free of charge. However, fees are charged for certain diagnostic tests in accordance with government regulations," he said.
The director said general anaesthesia was not necessary for every eye surgery involving heart patients. Many procedures could be performed using local anaesthesia or anaesthetic eye drops.
However, some procedures, including retinal surgery and certain eye muscle operations, may require general anaesthesia. Heart patients undergoing such procedures may need ICU support, he said.
Patients with heart conditions who require general anaesthesia for eye surgery are advised to undergo the procedures at other government medical college hospitals equipped with ICU facilities, he added.
Asked about the difficulties patients face in securing appointments at those hospitals, Dr Qadir said patient numbers exceeded available capacity, resulting in long waiting periods.
Regarding plans to establish an ICU, he said: "Setting up an ICU is not something I can do alone. It requires adequate space, manpower and technicians. I will certainly take the initiative if there is an opportunity to establish one through discussions with the Ministry of Health."
The National Institute of Ophthalmology and Hospital began its journey in 1979 with 100 beds inside the Shaheed Suhrawardy Hospital Complex in Sher-e-Bangla Nagar, Dhaka. In December 2007, it moved to its own premises in Agargaon and began operating as a 250-bed hospital.
It is now one of the country's leading specialised and referral centres for eye care.
According to hospital sources, around 4,000 patients visit its outpatient department every day. They receive various diagnostic and treatment services for a nominal ticket fee of Tk10.
The hospital also accommodates an average of 220 to 250 inpatients daily. Its outpatient and emergency departments together provide services to around 600,000 to 700,000 patients annually.
To cater to this large number of patients, the hospital performs an average of 60 to 80 minor and major surgeries every day, including around 50 to 60 phacoemulsification procedures for cataract treatment.
Overall, approximately 27,000 to 28,000 eye surgeries are performed at the hospital each year.
The hospital currently has 250 beds. To cope with the growing patient load, there are plans to expand the facility into a 10-storey building and increase its capacity to 500 beds, the director said.

item.title: Factory closures, clashes disrupt garment operations in Ashulia, Gazipur
item.description:
Demands for a Tk30,000 monthly minimum wage triggered protests across major garment-producing areas on Saturday, disrupting operations at dozens of factories in Ashulia and Gazipur and leading to clashes between workers and police.
At least 30 factories in Ashulia and 18 to 20 in Kaliakair, Gazipur, declared holidays amid the unrest. Clashes left at least five industrial police personnel and several garment workers injured, while police recovered three crude bomb-like objects from the Dhaka-Tangail Highway in Ashulia.
Superintendent of Police of Ashulia Industrial Police-1 Mohammad Mominul Islam Bhuiyan confirmed the factory closures at around 1:45pm on Saturday.
Police sources said workers of Naim Knitwear first stopped working inside the factory in the Kathgara area in the morning. They later came out and staged protests, throwing bricks at several nearby factories.
At one stage, workers and police engaged in chases and counter-chases.
During a visit on Saturday afternoon, a tense situation was observed in Nishchintapur, Kathgara, Zirabo and Narsinghpur areas of Ashulia in Savar.
Speaking to workers, it was learnt that employees of Newage Apparels and Newage Garments in Nishchintapur began a work stoppage in the morning, demanding a minimum wage of Tk30,000, an end to blacklisting and a halt to worker layoffs.
Later, workers at Al-Muslim, Continental and AR Jeans in Kathgara, Naim Sweater and FNF Garments in Narsinghpur, and Trouser Line in Zirabo also staged protests.
At noon, garment workers gathered in Nishchintapur. When police attempted to disperse them, clashes involving chases and counter-chases broke out.
Police later fired tear gas, prompting workers to throw bricks at them. At least 5 industrial police personnel were injured, while several garment workers also sustained injuries.
Mohammad Mominul Islam Bhuiyan said the situation remained tense as workers took positions at different locations and could prevent employees at other factories from working.
He said: “The situation is not very good now due to the workers' protests. Workers are taking positions at different locations. They may obstruct workers at other factories from working. We are trying to explain the situation to the workers. So far, at least 30 garment factories have declared holidays. A police member was hit on the head by bricks thrown by protesters and has been admitted to hospital.”
Inspector (Investigation) of Ashulia police station Harun-or-Rashid said: “Since morning, workers have been staging protests and work stoppages in Zirabo, Nishchintapur and Kathgara. However, the situation was brought under control at noon.”
Khairul Mamun, legal affairs secretary of the Bangladesh Garments and Sweaters Workers Trade Union Centre, said setting the minimum wage at Tk30,000 was a longstanding demand of workers.
He added that workers must not be blacklisted or dismissed arbitrarily.
Khairul Mamun said the labor minister had announced that a wage board would be formed within October, but the process had not started, creating resentment among workers.
He said a meeting at the Ministry of Labor on Friday night decided that the process of forming the minimum wage board would begin by next Sunday. However, the message had not properly reached the workers, prompting continued protests.
A worker at Newage Apparels, speaking on condition of anonymity, said: “The prices of everything have increased, but our wages have not. If our wages are not increased, how will we support our families?”
Meanwhile, industrial police recovered 3 crude bomb-like objects from the Dhaka-Tangail Highway in Ashulia at noon.
The objects were found in front of a factory belonging to Nassa Group in the Nishchintapur area.
Mohammad Mominul Islam said: “The matter has been reported to the Bangladesh Police's Anti-Terrorism Unit (ATU). They will come to the scene and take further steps.”
Meanwhile, at least 18-20 factories declared holidays following clashes between police and garment workers protesting for wage increases near the Dhaka-Tangail Highway in Kaliakair, Gazipur.
Authorities declared holidays at all garment factories along the 13-kilometer stretch from Konabari to Chandra.
Gazipur Industrial Police Superintendent Amjad Hossain confirmed the information on Saturday afternoon.

item.title: Garment workers block Dhaka-Tangail highway, clash with police
item.description:
Garment workers blocked the Dhaka-Tangail highway again for nearly three hours on Saturday, demanding a minimum monthly wage of Tk30,000, triggering clashes with police.
The clashes broke out around 5:30pm on Saturday when police attempted to disperse the protesters. Police fired tear gas and sound grenades, leaving several people injured.
Earlier, workers had blocked the highway from around 2:30pm, triggering severe traffic congestion. To prevent further unrest, authorities declared holidays at least 12 factories in the area.
The blockade brought traffic to a complete standstill on the highway, causing widespread suffering for commuters.
According to police and local sources, workers of Interstop factory began protesting by blocking the Dhaka-Tangail highway in the Chandra Palli Bidyut area of Kaliakair Upazila around 2:30pm on Saturday. Workers from several other factories later joined the protest.
During the demonstration, the workers placed sacks filled with soil, wood and bamboo on the highway and set them on fire, bringing traffic to a standstill along several kilometres of the road.
The protesting workers said they had been urging factory authorities to increase their wages and benefits over the past few days.
However, as the authorities failed to reach a decision on their demands, the workers became agitated, stopped working and eventually took to the streets.
According to industrial police and workers, demonstrations demanding higher wages have been continuing for the past two weeks in Konabari, Mouchak and several other areas. Although the government has decided to form a new wage board to review workers' salaries, labour unrest has persisted at several factories.
On Saturday, during the lunch break, workers of Interstop factory refused to resume work and took to the Dhaka-Tangail highway. They later blocked the road by placing sacks of waste and debris from nearby areas on it.
Workers of the neighbouring Divine Textile factory subsequently joined the protest, spreading labour unrest among factories from Chandra to Konabari.
In response to the escalating situation, authorities declared holidays at 12 factories in the area.
After receiving reports of the protest, police from the local police station and industrial police rushed to the scene and tried to bring the situation under control by persuading the workers to end their demonstration.
The blockade began around 2:30pm, causing severe inconvenience to passengers and transport workers. At around 5:30pm, tensions escalated into clashes when police attempted to remove the workers from the highway. Police fired tear gas shells to disperse the protesters, who retaliated by throwing bricks and stones at law enforcers, turning the area into a virtual battleground.
The highway blockade also left thousands of passengers and drivers stranded. Police repeatedly urged the workers to clear the road to ease public suffering, but they ignored the appeals and continued their demonstration, setting fires on the highway.
Police also fired sound grenades in an attempt to disperse the protesters and restore normalcy. Clashes between workers and police continued, spreading panic across the area.
Kaliakair Police Station Officer-in-Charge Shahidul Islam said police were trying to calm the workers and bring the situation under control.
"Authorities have declared holidays at 10 to 12 nearby factories. We have arrived at the scene to pacify the workers and are trying to contain the clashes," he said.
Gazipur Industrial Police Superintendent Mohammad Amzad Hossain said the situation had remained normal in the morning, but workers from several factories joined the protest in the afternoon.
"The workers had been blocking the Dhaka-Tangail highway in the Palli Bidyut area for about an hour. When police tried to remove them, they hurled bricks and stones at law enforcers, triggering clashes. We are trying to bring the situation under control," he said.

item.title: Al-Arafah Islami Bank holds Town Hall Meeting for Dhaka South Zone
item.description:

At the event, the bank’s chairman Badiur Rahman and directors Engr Khandaker Mesbah Uddin Ahmed and Khwaja Shahriar delivered speeches as special guests.
Managing director of the bank Mohd Rafat Ullah Khan presided over the meeting on Saturday, October 31.
The bank’s deputy managing directors Md Fazlur Rahman Chowdhury, Md Asaduzzaman Bhuiyan, Md Aminul Islam Bhuiyan, SM Abu Jafar, and Syed Abul Hashem were present at the event.
Chairman Badiur Rahman said: “Al-Arafah Islami Bank has moved forward over the years with the trust and confidence of its customers. At this juncture, we want to move ahead with renewed enthusiasm in a stronger and more organized manner. We must further strengthen the Bank’s position through quality business expansion, deposit growth, improved customer service and sustainable growth. Above all, every activity of the bank must be conducted with the highest importance given to the principles and values of Shariah.”
Managing director Mohd Rafat Ullah Khan said: “All of us associated with this institution are members of one family. This town hall meeting serves as an important platform for strengthening our mutual connection, reviewing our progress and determining our future course of action.”
He also instructed the branch managers to pay greater attention to achieving their business targets across various areas.
He placed particular emphasis on the recovery of classified investments and cost reduction as the bank’s key priorities in the current period.
The event was moderated by the bank’s senior executive vice president and head of GSD Engr Md Habib Ullah.

item.title: Home minister: Future political course must reflect people's will
item.description:
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed on Saturday said the country's future political course must be shaped in line with the people's aspirations and national will to ensure a sustainable democratic system.
He stressed the need for broad political consensus and dialogue among all stakeholders, including opposition parties, to determine the country's future direction and introduce reforms that would prevent the emergence of authoritarian rule.
He made the remarks at a seminar titled "Constitutional Crisis in Post-Independence Bangladesh and BAKSAL", the first in the "Democratic Journey" seminar series organized by the July Memorial Museum in Dhaka.
He said constitutional reforms should reflect the aspirations of the July mass uprising and the expectations of the younger generation, with a focus on establishing institutional checks and balances to ensure that no individual or government could exercise unchecked power.
The minister said one of the government's key goals is to establish effective watchdog institutions to protect democracy.
These include ensuring judicial independence, maintaining an impartial Election Commission, introducing a permanent legal framework for a caretaker government system and safeguarding press freedom.
The seminar was chaired by Ehsan Mahmud, director general of the July Memorial Museum, while former interim government Law Adviser Asif Nazrul delivered the keynote speech.
Firoz Ahmed, a former member of the Constitution Reform Commission, and Supreme Court lawyer Habibur Rahman also took part in the discussion.
Salahuddin said that although the Constitution had laid down clear provisions for running the state after independence, the introduction of a one-party system through BAKSAL in 1975 had paved the way for a constitutional crisis and authoritarian rule.
He said the abolition of the caretaker government system through the 15th Amendment in 2011 was a major factor behind the erosion of democracy and the rise of fascist forces in the post-BAKSAL period.
This political course eventually led to the July 2024 mass uprising, when students and people from different walks of life united to bring down the authoritarian regime, he added.
The minister said the country's future political system must reflect the will of the people.
On judicial reforms, he said independence of the judiciary alone was not enough; accountability was also necessary to ensure that no institution of the state could exercise unchecked power.
He also stressed the need for dialogue and political consensus among all stakeholders, including opposition parties, on various reform proposals, including the introduction of an upper house, proportional representation in elections and the holding of referendums.
The minister said the government had no intention of pursuing political vendettas or creating divisions.
He called for unity among political parties and people, saying broad political consensus, guided by the spirit of the July mass uprising and the aspirations of the younger generation, was essential to building a democratic and prosperous Bangladesh.

item.title: Milon calls for climate-resilient, sustainable agriculture
item.description:
Education and Primary and Mass Education Minister AKM Ehsanul Hoque Milon Saturday stressed the need to build a sustainable and climate-resilient agricultural system to tackle the challenges ahead.
Milon made the remarks while addressing the inaugural session of the 25th Conference of the Bangladesh Society of Agronomy as chief guest at the Bangladesh Agricultural Research Council auditorium in the capital.
"We have made remarkable progress in agricultural production. But the challenge ahead is not just about boosting output; we must keep pace with limited resources, climate change and rapidly evolving technologies," the minister said.
He said efforts must focus on ensuring higher yields from the same land at lower costs, with better quality and environmental sustainability.
Noting that scientists and researchers publish numerous papers and develop new technologies every year, the minister said the reach of such innovations must be measured by how many farmers actually benefit from them.
"Our agricultural universities must not remain mere degree-awarding institutions. They need to emerge stronger as hubs of innovation, problem-solving and transformation of the agriculture sector," he added.
Milon also underscored the need for a skilled workforce for a modern agricultural economy, particularly in operating farm machinery, irrigation technology and food processing.
He said Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) can play a vital role in building these skills.

item.title: Bangladeshi tech entrepreneur Juman Khan's organization now working globally
item.description:
Entrepreneur Juman Khan, co-founder of International Technology of Bangladesh (ITB), is leading the company’s growing presence in the international digital services market, with the organization now working with clients from different countries around the world.
Khan co-founded International Technology of Bangladesh on April 9 last year with the vision of providing professional digital and social media services to clients both in Bangladesh and internationally.
Since its establishment, ITB has expanded its services to include digital marketing, web design, app development, search engine optimization (SEO), Facebook marketing, Instagram marketing, and other social media solutions.
Under the leadership and guidance of Juman Khan, the company has built a growing international client base.
Its clients include well-known individuals and professionals from different sectors, including actors, actresses, sports personalities, singers, administrative officials, members of parliament, and ministers.
At present, around 38 employees are working at International Technology of Bangladesh, with monthly earnings ranging from approximately Tk20,000 to Tk50,000.
According to a company official, ITB currently handles more projects for international clients than for clients in Bangladesh.
“More than 70% of our work is carried out for clients outside Bangladesh. We believe our international work also contributes to the country’s economy. We have reached this position because of the proper guidance and leadership of Juman Khan, the founder and CEO of our organization,” the official said.
The official also said that Juman Khan has created opportunities for students to work alongside their studies, allowing many of them to gain professional experience while also supporting their families financially.
An ITB client from the Philippines also praised the company’s services and the leadership of Juman Khan.
“Working with International Technology of Bangladesh has helped my business move significantly forward in the Philippines. I have worked with many organizations before, but I have never received this level of service. Their marketing work is performing very well, and the quality of their services is excellent. They take every assignment seriously and complete the work professionally, often ahead of schedule,” the client said.
Speaking about his philosophy toward work, Juman Khan, co-founder and CEO of International Technology of Bangladesh, said: “We take every client’s work very seriously, whether the work is small or large. I believe every job should be given equal importance. If you have respect and passion for your work, you can achieve great things even through small tasks.”
With Juman Khan at the helm, International Technology of Bangladesh is continuing to expand its international operations while creating employment opportunities for young people in Bangladesh.
The company aims to further strengthen its position in the global digital services market and showcase the skills and capabilities of Bangladeshi digital professionals to clients around the world.

item.title: Nitai Roy: Bangladesh’s cultural heritage to be promoted in 51 countries
item.description:
The government has planned to showcase Bangladesh's thousand-year-old cultural heritage to the world through cultural diplomacy with 51 countries, Cultural Affairs Minister Nitai Roy Chowdhury said on Saturday.
The government is working continuously to promote the country's arts and culture since the declaration of Nazrul Year, he said.
The minister made the remarks while exchanging views with cultural activists at a meeting organised by Chuadanga Zila Parishad at the conference room of Chuadanga Circuit House.
Initiatives have also been taken to introduce the younger generation to arts and culture through various programmes at educational institutions across the country, he added.
Nitai Roy Chowdhury said Bangladesh has a rich cultural heritage spanning thousands of years, and the government is placing special emphasis on cultural diplomacy to introduce the country's arts, traditions and heritage to people in other countries.
He also announced that Baul festivals would be organised across the country from now on. Traditional folk music, Bhatiyali songs and boat races have been included in the ministry's cultural heritage initiatives, he said.
The government has also taken steps to revive and promote traditional rural games such as Dariabandha, Ha-du-du, Kabaddi and Lathi Khela, the minister added. He said the Prime Minister had been providing immense encouragement for the development of the country's cultural sector.
Cultural activists from Chuadanga raised various demands concerning the development of the district's cultural sector, expansion of artistic activities and promotion of local cultural organisations.
They later submitted a memorandum to the minister outlining their demands for the overall development of culture in the district.
Presided over by Chuadanga Zila Parishad Administrator and District unit BNP General Secretary Sharifuzzaman Sharif, the meeting was attended by local cultural activists and representatives of different organisations.

item.title: Minister: Strong agricultural economy key to national economic growth
item.description:
Agriculture, Fisheries and Livestock Minister Mohammad Amin Ur Rashid on Saturday said the country’s economic strength depends on strengthening its agricultural economy, as most people in Bangladesh are directly or indirectly involved in the sector.
“The government believes that a strong agricultural economy will lead to a strong national economy,” he said, adding that modern technology was essential to reducing post-harvest losses and expanding agricultural exports.
The minister was speaking at the inauguration of the country’s first large-scale Gamma Irradiation Centre at the Bangladesh Institute of Nuclear Agriculture (BINA) Regional Research Centre in Bhabanipur of Gazipur.
He said the government was working to reduce dependence on imported agricultural products, particularly onions, and expressed hope that Bangladesh would no longer need to import onions in the future.
The 500,000-curie-capacity facility will use gamma irradiation technology to eliminate harmful microorganisms, prevent spoilage, and extend the shelf life of agricultural products, including onions, potatoes, mangoes, jackfruits, pineapples, and vegetables.
The minister said Bangladesh produced high-quality mangoes and other fruits, but their limited shelf life and difficulties meeting international safety standards had restricted export opportunities.
He said the new technology would help make agricultural products safer and more suitable for international markets, including Australia, China, Pakistan and Europe, where demand for Bangladeshi fruits was growing.
“Bangladesh is an agriculture-based country, yet agricultural products have not become one of its leading export items. Technological limitations are among the main reasons,” he said.
Rashid stressed that the centre's success would depend not only on investment and machinery but also on efficient management and skilled personnel. He said the government planned to establish similar facilities across the country to ensure better market access and fair prices for farmers.
Highlighting food safety, he said the government was also testing the quality of imported food products and would take steps to stop imports of items considered harmful to public health.
According to BINA, China's state-owned China Isotope and Radiation Corporation received the contract to build the centre through an international tender in 2024.
